query: How can melting temperature, enthalpy and entropy of fusion, volume change at melting, and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties be determined accurately and efficiently across the high-entropy-alloy family? State the physical rationale, expected quantitative performance, range of applicability, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive validation result that would rule out the proposed approach.

generation.hypothesis: An integrated, high‐throughput framework that couples CALPHAD-based thermodynamic modeling with machine learning corrections derived from targeted experimental measurements can accurately and efficiently predict the liquidus properties (melting temperature, fusion enthalpy and entropy, volume change on melting, and other liquid-phase thermodynamic properties) across the high-entropy alloy (HEA) family.
generation.material_initial_state: High-entropy alloys in their as-cast or homogenized single-phase (or well‐characterized multiphase) state, typically exhibiting high configurational entropy and simple BCC or FCC structures.
generation.intervention: Develop and deploy a computational protocol that leverages high-throughput CALPHAD calculations augmented with data-driven (machine learning) correction factors, followed by selective experimental validation (e.g., DSC, DTA, high-temperature XRD) to refine the model predictions.
generation.conditions: Measurements and calculations under controlled thermal conditions (e.g., near-equilibrium melting experiments) over a representative compositional range (typically equiatomic or near-equiatomic mixtures with ≥5 principal elements) where CALPHAD databases are sufficiently reliable.
generation.structural_mediator: Local atomic configurations and short-range order—which affect mixing enthalpy, entropy contributions, and atomic size differences—mediate the liquid-phase thermodynamic behavior during melting.
generation.mechanism: By using established thermodynamic rules (e.g., mixing enthalpy, configurational entropy, volume effects) combined with modern computational screening, the framework assigns quantitative estimates to melting properties. Machine learning corrections account for deviations arising from complex interactions not fully captured by current CALPHAD databases, thereby refining the property predictions.
generation.predicted_outcome: The framework should predict melting temperatures, fusion enthalpies and entropies, and melting volume changes within a narrow error margin (e.g., ±5–10%) relative to high-resolution experimental measurements across diverse HEA compositions.
generation.baseline: Traditional methods rely on labor-intensive, one-by-one experimental measurements (e.g., DSC) or limited CALPHAD evaluations, which are not efficient for mapping the vast compositional space of HEAs.
generation.boundary: This approach is expected to be most applicable for HEA systems where the constituent elements and interactions are well-represented in existing thermodynamic databases; predictions may be less reliable for systems exhibiting strong electronic or magnetic effects or in regions where experimental data is scarce.
generation.uncertainty: There remains uncertainty in regions of the composition space with limited experimental calibration data and in cases where emergent phenomena (e.g., unexpected liquid-phase ordering or phase separation) may occur, potentially exceeding the predictive scope of current CALPHAD models.

falsification_experiment.design: Select a set of HEA compositions spanning the typical compositional space (e.g., varying equiatomic ratios within 5–7 element systems) and use high-resolution, high-throughput thermal analysis (such as differential scanning calorimetry and in situ high-temperature XRD) to accurately measure melting temperatures, enthalpies, entropies of fusion, and volume changes at melting. Independently, use the proposed computational framework to predict these properties. A statistical comparison between predicted and experimentally measured values will then be performed.
measurements: Fusion enthalpy and entropy from calorimetric data
Volume change upon melting measured by high-temperature dilatometry
Liquid-phase properties from in situ high-temperature XRD or neutron scattering
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If, for more than 30% of the tested compositions, the predicted values deviate from the experimentally measured values by more than 10%, then the proposed framework is deemed inadequate for accurate determination and is falsified.

Abstract Developing affordable and light high-temperature materials alternative to Ni-base superalloys has significantly increased the efforts in designing advanced ferritic superalloys. However, currently developed ferritic superalloys still exhibit low high-temperature strengths, which limits their usage. Here we use a CALPHAD-based high-throughput computational method to design light, strong, and low-cost high-entropy alloys for elevated-temperature applications. Through the high-throughput screening, precipitation-strengthened lightweight high-entropy alloys are discovered from thousands of initial compositions, which exhibit enhanced strengths compared to other counterparts at room and elevated temperatures. The experimental and theoretical understanding of both successful and failed cases in their strengthening mechanisms and order-disorder transitions further improves the accuracy of the thermodynamic database of the discovered alloy system.
